subjects.title: Team environment, rollout and spend
learn: A team environment is a shared project-level baseline: shared CLAUDE.md, agreed tools and MCP servers, and a permission posture, reviewed and versioned.
Rollout runs through a champion per team who gets access first, proves a real workflow, then seeds adoption batch by batch.
Spend posture is set before the first bill: model defaults, allowlists, effort guidance and spend, rate or per-user caps.
Server-managed settings come from Anthropic's servers on authentication, refresh hourly, and are not a Skills distribution path.
Shaping layers (CLAUDE.md, skills, subagents, MCP) differ from governing layers (hooks, permissions, sandboxing); six permission modes control prompting.
traps: All-hands switch-on: team adoption rarely succeeds that way; without champions absorbing early friction, the Architect becomes the only person answering questions.
Inherited spend defaults: unmanaged model choice quietly multiplies a costlier tier across every member.
Settings versus Skills: server-managed settings do not distribute Skills.
Prompt versus gate: CLAUDE.md shapes behavior, only hooks guarantee a check cannot be skipped.
Mode mix-ups: bypassPermissions is for containers or CI only; dontAsk is the locked-down CI mode.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a team environment for Claude Code?
options: Each developer's personal setup, tuned over time and shared informally between colleagues on request
A reviewed, versioned project baseline: shared CLAUDE.md, agreed tools and MCP servers, and a permission posture
A vendor-supplied default configuration the team adopts unchanged and never customizes locally
A single administrator's configuration that every developer's session inherits without anyone reviewing it
questions.explanation: A team environment is a shared project-level baseline that can be reviewed, versioned and improved once for everyone. Personal setups drift apart, which is exactly what the baseline prevents.
questions.mnemonic: One baseline, reviewed and versioned; personal setups drift.

questions.stem: An organization wants Claude Code adopted across several engineering teams. Which rollout approach is most likely to succeed?
options: Switch everyone on together so all teams begin from the same day
Let the keenest volunteers adopt it and others follow whenever they choose
Champion per team gets access first, proves a real workflow, then seeds batches
Have the Architect run central training for every team and answer all questions personally
questions.explanation: Team adoption rarely succeeds as a single all-hands switch-on. A champion per team is granted access first, proves the workflow in practice and seeds adoption batch by batch, absorbing early friction along the way. Central training alone leaves the Architect as the only person who can answer questions.
questions.mnemonic: One champion per team proves it first, then batches follow.

questions.stem: Which TWO responsibilities does a department champion take on during rollout? Select TWO.
options: Waits for the broad rollout before trying the workflow in practice
Owns organization billing and sets the shared per-user spend caps
Approves every permission-mode change across the whole organization
Absorbs early friction and builds local examples for peers
Acts as first-line support so the Architect is not the sole answerer
questions.explanation: The champion absorbs early friction, builds local examples, and becomes first-line support. Spend caps and permission posture remain admin and Architect decisions, and a champion who waits defeats the purpose.
questions.mnemonic: Champions soak up friction and answer first.

questions.stem: When should admins set model defaults, model allowlists, effort guidance and spend caps for a team?
options: Only for champions, since later batches inherit them automatically
Once the champion batch has shown real usage patterns
Before the first bill, set intentionally rather than inherited as defaults
After the first monthly bill shows which teams overspent
questions.explanation: Spend posture is part of team setup and must be decided up front. Waiting for a bill means the cost has already multiplied across every member and request.
questions.mnemonic: Set the guardrails before the bill, not after.

questions.stem: A 60-developer team's Claude spend doubled in a month with no growth in usage. Developers had been free to pick any model for every task. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Unmanaged model choice sending routine work to a costlier tier, multiplied
Server-managed settings refreshing hourly and re-running sessions repeatedly
Too many champions generating examples that every later batch then reran
Permission modes prompting too often and lengthening every single session
questions.explanation: Leaving model choice unmanaged quietly sends work to a more capable, more expensive tier than needed, and at team scale that choice multiplies across every member and request. Defaults, allowlists and caps prevent it.
questions.mnemonic: One unmanaged model pick, times every developer.

questions.stem: How are server-managed settings for Claude Code delivered?
options: Read from Organization settings > Skills at the start of every session
From Anthropic's servers on authentication, refreshed on an hourly polling cycle
Committed to .claude/ in the repository and applied at checkout
Pushed once at install time and changed only when an admin re-uploads
questions.explanation: Server-managed settings come from Anthropic's servers when users authenticate and refresh hourly. The repository and Skills settings are different channels.
questions.mnemonic: Authenticate, fetch, refresh hourly: settings from the server.

questions.stem: A colleague proposes using server-managed settings to roll out the team's commit-message skill to every engineer. What is the best response?
options: It is a settings mechanism, not Skills distribution; use a plugin, org Skill or project Skill
It works well, and the hourly refresh gives the skill built-in version rollback for free
It works only for API Skills, which are the sole Skills that settings can carry
It is correct, provided the skill is also placed in the repository's CLAUDE.md file
questions.explanation: Server-managed settings centrally manage Claude Code configuration but are not a way to distribute Skills. Skills go through org-provisioning, plugins, project .claude/skills/ or the API.
questions.mnemonic: Settings are not Skills: different pipe.

questions.stem: A team needs a guarantee that a check runs before a tool executes and that the agent cannot skip it. Which Claude Code layer fits?
options: An MCP server exposing the check
A subagent with a restricted prompt
CLAUDE.md standing instructions
A hook on the lifecycle event
questions.explanation: Hooks are scripts on lifecycle events that act as deterministic gates, so the guarantee comes from code rather than prompting. CLAUDE.md and subagents shape behavior but do not enforce it.
questions.mnemonic: Prompts persuade; hooks enforce.

questions.stem: Which TWO Claude Code layers govern what the agent is allowed to touch, rather than shaping what it knows and does? Select TWO.
options: Hooks firing on lifecycle events
CLAUDE.md standing project instructions
Subagents with isolated context windows
Permission boundaries and approval flows
MCP servers exposing external tools
questions.explanation: Governing layers are hooks, permissions and approval flows, and sandboxing. CLAUDE.md, skills, subagents and MCP servers are shaping layers.
questions.mnemonic: Shape: know and do. Govern: touch and gate.

questions.stem: Which permission mode suits a locked-down CI job that should run only what the allow rules explicitly cover?
options: plan mode
default
acceptEdits
dontAsk
questions.explanation: dontAsk auto-denies anything that would prompt and runs only what allow rules cover, making it the mode for locked-down CI. Default prompts before each action, which CI cannot answer.
questions.mnemonic: dontAsk: no asking, only allow-list, built for CI.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Claude Code permission modes are accurate? Select TWO.
options: acceptEdits approves every Bash command of any kind as well as all file edits
bypassPermissions skips all checks and is scoped to containers or CI only
Default mode approves common filesystem commands without prompting the user at all
Plan mode locks the session to read-only until the user approves a plan
questions.explanation: Plan mode is read-only until a plan is approved, and bypassPermissions skips every check so it belongs only in containers or CI. acceptEdits covers edits and common filesystem commands only, and default asks before each action.
questions.mnemonic: Plan reads, bypass only in boxes.

questions.stem: An admin wants every new Claude Code session to begin on a mid-tier model, while still letting developers switch to a stronger model when a task needs it. Which spend guardrail sets the starting model?
options: A per-user spend cap applied across the whole team
A model default, which fixes the model a session starts on
A model allowlist naming which models the team may use
Effort guidance setting how hard the model works per task
questions.explanation: The model default decides which model a session starts on. An allowlist or restriction governs which models the team may switch to, so it limits choice rather than setting the starting point; caps and effort guidance bound consumption and effort.
questions.mnemonic: Default is where you start; allowlist is where you may go.

questions.stem: A team lead wants to stop developers switching to the most expensive model tier and to bound how much any single person can consume. Which TWO spend guardrails address these needs? Select TWO.
options: Model allowlists and restrictions on which models the team may switch to
Per-user caps that keep each person's consumption within a set bound
A shared CLAUDE.md that asks developers to prefer cheaper models
A model default that sets which model each session starts on
Effort guidance describing how hard the model should work on a task
questions.explanation: Allowlists and restrictions control which models people may switch to, and per-user caps bound individual consumption. A model default only sets the starting model, so developers can still switch up; a CLAUDE.md request is guidance, not a guardrail.
questions.mnemonic: Allowlist fences the tiers; per-user cap fences the person.

questions.stem: A manager questions spending time on a shared configuration, a rollout plan and skills packaging before developers start using Claude Code. Which response best reflects the cost trade-off?
options: It is overhead worth skipping for small teams, who can each tune their own personal setups
It should wait until the first bill shows which teams actually use the tool
It costs setup time now, but is far cheaper than reconciling drifted configurations later
It only pays off for teams that call Claude through API Skills in products
questions.explanation: Standing up a team environment costs setup time for shared config, a rollout plan and skills packaging, but it is far cheaper than later reconciling many individual configurations that have drifted apart. Waiting for the first bill also contradicts setting the spend posture up front.
questions.mnemonic: Pay setup once now, or reconcile drifted configs later.

subjects.title: Distributing Skills to a team
learn: Org-provisioned Skills reach everyone at once; users can toggle them off but not remove them; no version pinning or native rollback, so updates need manual re-upload.
Plugins assigned to a group or org give group targeting, install preferences and version-controlled updates from a connected repo: the strongest governance.
Claude Code project Skills live in .claude/skills/, version and roll back with the repo, and are scoped to its projects.
API Skills are called programmatically by partner products, support explicit version pinning, and are machine-to-machine.
Choose by who needs access and how much control and rollback is needed; packaging a local practice makes it a team standard.
traps: Unversioned shared asset: a skill or config with no versioning or rollback lets one bad change reach the whole team before anyone can stop it.
Wrong channel: server-managed settings are not a Skills distribution path.
Org-wide overshoot: org-provisioned reaches everyone and cannot be natively rolled back.
Plugin-only assumption: API Skills and project Skills also have a path back to a prior version.
Missing owner: shared assets need a named owner, not just a distribution path.

questions.stem: A Skill uploaded under Organization settings > Skills reaches everyone at once. What can individual users do with it?
options: Pin it to a specific version
Toggle it off but not remove it
Remove it from their own account permanently
Roll it back to the earlier version
questions.explanation: Org-provisioned Skills are owner-managed: users can toggle individual skills off but cannot remove them. There is no version pinning or native rollback.
questions.mnemonic: Toggle off, never remove: owner holds the switch.

questions.stem: An org-provisioned Skill gets a bad edit and every employee sees degraded output. What is the recovery path?
options: Manually re-upload a corrected version, as no pinning or rollback exists
Roll back natively to the last pinned version of the skill
Reassign the plugin to a different group of employees
Wait for the hourly settings refresh to restore the earlier version
questions.explanation: Org-provisioned Skills lack version pinning and native rollback, so updates and fixes require manual re-upload. The hourly refresh belongs to server-managed settings, not Skills.
questions.mnemonic: Org-wide upload: fix means re-upload by hand.

questions.stem: Which Skills distribution mechanism offers the strongest governance for group-scoped distribution?
options: An API Skill called programmatically from a partner's own product
A plugin assigned to a group, with install preferences and versioned updates
A Claude Code project Skill stored under .claude/skills/ in the repository
An org-provisioned Skill uploaded under Organization settings > Skills
questions.explanation: Plugins combine group targeting, install preferences and version-controlled updates from a connected repository. Org-provisioned Skills lack pinning and rollback.
questions.mnemonic: Plugin: group, preference, version. The governed route.

questions.stem: Which TWO capabilities does distributing Skills through a plugin provide? Select TWO.
options: Skills that exist only as files in a project's .claude/skills/ folder
Version-controlled updates from a connected repository
Install preferences such as required, installed-by-default, available or not available
Users removing the plugin permanently from the organization
Explicit version pinning inside a Messages API container
questions.explanation: Plugins offer install preferences and version-controlled updates from a connected repo, plus group targeting. Container version pinning belongs to API Skills and .claude/skills/ files are project Skills.
questions.mnemonic: Plugin knobs: install preference plus repo-versioned updates.

questions.stem: One team wants a coding convention skill shared across its own repositories, versioned with the code. Which mechanism fits?
options: An API Skill with explicit version pinning
Organization settings > Skills upload
A Claude Code project Skill in .claude/skills/
A plugin assigned to the whole organization
questions.explanation: Project Skills are filesystem artifacts in the repo, so they version with it, are scoped to the projects that carry them, and roll back with the repository.
questions.mnemonic: Skills in the repo travel and roll back with the repo.

questions.stem: A partner's own product calls a capability programmatically and needs to pin an exact version. Which mechanism fits?
options: Plugin installed by default
API Skill
Server-managed settings
Org-provisioned Skill
questions.explanation: API Skills are called programmatically in machine-to-machine reuse and support explicit version pinning, governed in the calling system.
questions.mnemonic: API Skill: machine caller, pinned version.

questions.stem: A data-science group needs a shared analysis procedure that only its members receive, updated from a connected repository, with a way back if an update misbehaves. Which distribution choice fits best?
options: Upload it under Organization settings > Skills so it reaches the group at once
Have each member copy it into a personal skills folder and update it by hand
Deliver it through server-managed settings on the hourly polling cycle
Bundle it in a group-assigned plugin and decide who can update or revoke it
questions.explanation: Group targeting, version-controlled updates from a connected repository and a path back are plugin features, and per-asset governance decides who can update and revoke it. An org-provisioned upload reaches everyone and has no native rollback; server-managed settings are not a Skills distribution path.
questions.mnemonic: Group scope plus rollback means plugin, governed per asset.

questions.stem: A team's shared Claude Code configuration is edited in place and pushed to every developer, with no version history and no way to revert. What is the biggest risk of this setup?
options: Spend caps run out sooner because every developer reloads the full configuration daily
Developers lose the ability to toggle the configuration off for themselves
One bad change propagates to the whole team before anyone can stop it
Only the configuration's original author can start sessions that apply its settings
questions.explanation: The biggest failure mode in team setup is a shared asset, whether a skill or a config, with no versioning or rollback, so one bad change reaches the whole team before anyone can stop it. Spend caps and user toggles are separate concerns.
questions.mnemonic: Shared, unversioned, no undo: one bad edit reaches everyone.

questions.stem: A legal team has three related Skills that only its own members should be able to use. How should the Architect distribute them?
options: Upload them org-wide and ask everyone else to toggle them off
Bundle them into one plugin and assign it to the legal group
Deliver them to the legal team through server-managed settings
Expose them as API Skills that the legal members call from their own sessions
questions.explanation: Bundling one or more Skills into a plugin assigned to a group means only that group's members can access them. An org-provisioned Skill reaches everyone and users can only toggle it off, not remove it; server-managed settings do not distribute Skills.
questions.mnemonic: Select members only? Plugin to the group, not upload to all.

questions.stem: Why is a shared Skill with no version and no rollback a liability for a team?
options: It consumes the team's spend caps faster than versioned shared assets would do
It cannot be toggled off by individual users once it is published
Once several people depend on it, one bad change reaches all before it stops
It only functions for the single Architect who originally wrote the skill
questions.explanation: The risk is propagation: a shared asset without versioning lets a single bad change spread to the whole team. Spend and toggling are separate concerns.
questions.mnemonic: No version, no way back: one slip hits all.

questions.stem: Why does packaging a team's local workflow as a distributable skill matter?
options: It turns undocumented know-how into one governed artifact updated through versioning
It lets individual developers keep their working practice private to themselves
It removes the need for any review of the workflow before release
It guarantees that the workflow itself never needs updating in future
questions.explanation: A packaged skill carries the procedure as one governed artifact instead of undocumented know-how, so a good local practice becomes a team standard.
questions.mnemonic: Package the practice, and it becomes the standard.

questions.stem: Besides plugins, which TWO mechanisms provide a path back to a prior version? Select TWO.
options: Server-managed settings, through their hourly refresh cycle
Org-provisioned Skills, through native built-in rollback
Claude Code project Skills, rolling back with the repository
API Skills, through explicit version pinning
questions.explanation: API Skills support explicit version pinning and project Skills roll back with the repo that carries them. Org-provisioned Skills have no native rollback and server-managed settings are not a Skills channel.
questions.mnemonic: Pin the API, revert the repo; org upload has neither.

questions.stem: An Architect is setting up distribution for a team's migration-checklist skill, a coding-conventions skill and a shared configuration. What is the hard part, and at what level should it be decided?
options: Which single mechanism suits every asset, decided once for the team
How to write each skill's prompt, decided by the department champions
Which model each skill runs on, decided by the spend posture
Who can reach, update and revoke each asset, decided per asset
questions.explanation: Distribution governance, meaning who can reach, update and revoke each shared asset, is the hard part and is decided on a per-asset basis. Picking one mechanism for everything ignores that assets differ in audience and in who should govern them.
questions.mnemonic: Reach, update, revoke: decide it asset by asset.

questions.stem: Which THREE considerations should drive the choice of distribution mechanism for a given team skill? Select THREE.
options: What the tool is and what job it performs
Which model tier the skill author tested it on
Who will use it, whether everyone or one group
Who has access to govern, update and revoke it
How long the SKILL.md instructions file has grown
questions.explanation: The mechanism should account for what the tool is, who uses it and who has access to govern it. The authoring model tier and the length of the instructions do not determine whether a skill should be org-wide, group-scoped, project-scoped or API-called.
questions.mnemonic: What, who uses, who governs: three questions pick the channel.

questions.stem: A security-awareness skill must reach every member of the organization, and its owner is comfortable managing updates by hand. Which distribution mechanism is the simplest fit?
options: A Claude Code project Skill committed to each repository
An org-provisioned Skill uploaded under Organization settings > Skills
An API Skill pinned to an explicit version in a container
Server-managed settings pushed on the hourly polling cycle
questions.explanation: An org-provisioned Skill becomes available to everyone in the organization at once, the simplest path when a capability genuinely should reach all members; updates require manual re-upload. Server-managed settings are a settings channel, not a Skills distribution path.
questions.mnemonic: Everyone, simply: upload it in Organization settings.

questions.stem: A partner's billing product calls a document-classification Skill programmatically through the Messages API. Where does governance of that Skill primarily live?
options: In the admin UI's install preferences for the group using it
In Organization settings, where users can toggle it off
In the calling system, with explicit version pinning, machine to machine
In the project repository's .claude/skills/ directory with the code
questions.explanation: API Skills are governed in the calling system and support explicit version pinning; their reuse is machine-to-machine rather than human-facing. Install preferences belong to plugins, and toggling belongs to org-provisioned Skills.
questions.mnemonic: API Skill: the caller governs, the version is pinned.

subjects.title: AI-assisted developer workflows and diligence
learn: Integrate assistance into the existing editor, review and test loop; team knowledge in people's heads becomes Skills and project configuration.
Stage discipline: writing code needs correctness and security review; reviewing treats AI flags as input; debugging verifies hypotheses against evidence.
Two failure modes: lumpy adoption (few heavy users) and stalling at basic chat; access is not adoption.
Diligence is responsibility for verifying and vouching for outputs; AI code meets the same standards as any other code.
The verification checklist covers correctness, security, maintainability and human understanding, backed by automated regression tests and eval gates.
traps: Green tests as proof: passing checks and plausible code do not show anyone understands the change.
Verdict trap: AI review flags are input to human judgment, not a verdict.
Access equals adoption: giving a team access does not move it past basic chat.
Lighter bar for AI: faster output tempts teams to review it less, which is judgment erosion.
Volume blind spot: cheaper code production raises review volume, so checks need to be automated.

questions.stem: Where does AI tooling pay off most for a development team?
options: In a weekly session where one expert runs prompts for others
In a standalone tool that replaces the team's review process
Inside the existing workflow: editor, review process and test loop
In a separate chat window developers visit when stuck
questions.explanation: Assistance should live inside the workflow the team already uses, with the Architect finding where it removes real friction. A separate chat window is visited occasionally and rarely changes the process.
questions.mnemonic: Put Claude in the loop, not in a side window.

questions.stem: How does integrating Claude into the workflow help encode a team's knowledge?
options: Conventions and procedures held in people's heads become Skills and project configuration
The model infers team standards automatically with no configuration needed at all
Reviewers store every past decision in chat history for later keyword search
Developers are asked to memorize prompts so the practice stays personal to them
questions.explanation: Conventions, review standards and procedures that usually live in heads become Skills and project config, so good practice travels with the tooling.
questions.mnemonic: Head knowledge becomes skills and config.

questions.stem: Claude drafts a first-pass implementation from a clear spec. Which review discipline does the writing stage still require?
options: None, if the spec was clear and the draft compiles
Only a style check, since logic follows from the spec
Review by a second AI session in place of the author's understanding
Correctness and security review, and the author must understand what was generated
questions.explanation: Generated code still needs correctness and security review, and the author must be able to explain it. A clear spec does not remove that duty.
questions.mnemonic: Clear spec, still review: author must understand.

questions.stem: Claude summarizes a diff and flags three likely issues in a pull request. How should the reviewer treat the flags?
options: As a final verdict that replaces human review
As unnecessary, since reviewing is the one stage AI cannot help
As input to the reviewer's judgment, not a verdict
As authoritative if more than two issues are flagged
questions.explanation: In the reviewing stage Claude summarizes, flags and explains, but human judgment makes the call. AI flags are input, not a verdict.
questions.mnemonic: Flags inform; humans decide.

questions.stem: Claude proposes a hypothesis for a production bug from a stack trace. What should the engineer do before acting on it?
options: Ask Claude to repeat the hypothesis more confidently
Escalate to the Architect before any investigation
Apply the fix at once, since the trace supports it
Verify the hypothesis against evidence before acting
questions.explanation: For debugging, Claude proposes hypotheses from a symptom and trace, but the engineer verifies against evidence before acting on them.
questions.mnemonic: Hypothesis first, evidence second, action third.

questions.stem: Two developers on a 30-person team use Claude heavily, while the rest barely touch it. Which failure mode is this, and what addresses it?
options: Spend overrun; tighten per-user caps and model allowlists
Lumpy adoption; spread usage through champions and batches
Stalling at basic chat; enable tool use and repo-aware assistance
Judgment erosion; add a verification checklist before merge
questions.explanation: Lumpy adoption means a few heavy users and many barely using it, so the gain never standardizes. The champion-and-batch rollout spreads usage deliberately.
questions.mnemonic: Few heavy users is lumpy; batches smooth it.

questions.stem: Why does leaving adoption to early adopters tend to fail?
options: Early adopters exhaust the team's shared spend caps before others start
Early adopters usually misuse the tooling and teach bad habits to others
The team never sees the real gain and the practice never standardizes
Their usage typically violates the shared project baseline configuration
questions.explanation: When a few use it heavily and the rest do not, the team does not realize the tool's real benefit and the practice is not standardized across it.
questions.mnemonic: Heavy few, idle many: no standard forms.

questions.stem: A team has full Claude access but uses it only as a question-answering box. Which TWO steps move them past basic chat? Select TWO.
options: Package repeated procedures as skills
Remove the shared CLAUDE.md to reduce friction
Wait for individual developers to find advanced features
Increase every user's model tier by default
Enable tool use and repository-aware assistance
questions.explanation: Access is not adoption. Teams stall until someone enables tool use, repository-aware assistance and packaged skills within current workflows.
questions.mnemonic: Access is not adoption: enable tools, repo, skills.

questions.stem: How is diligence defined for deployment in developer workflows?
options: Taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for outputs we use or share
Limiting AI assistance to non-production code that carries no risk
Reviewing only the code that fails automated tests during the pipeline
Using the most capable model available for every task in the workflow
questions.explanation: Deployment diligence is responsibility for verifying and vouching for the outputs used or shared, shown as holding AI code to the same standards as any other code.
questions.mnemonic: Diligence: verify it, vouch for it.

questions.stem: Which THREE belong among the four dimensions a verification checklist for AI-generated output must cover? Select THREE.
options: Human understanding of what shipped
Security of the generated change
Token cost per request at scale
Maintainability for the next engineer
Model latency percentile under load
questions.explanation: The four dimensions are correctness, security, maintainability and human understanding. Cost and latency are operational metrics, not part of that checklist.
questions.mnemonic: Correct, secure, maintainable, understood: four checks.

questions.stem: A team's checklist for AI-generated changes covers correctness, security and maintainability. Which item adds the missing fourth dimension?
options: The change was generated by the most capable model available
The diff stays under an agreed maximum size for review
The author can explain what the change does and why
A second AI session reviewed and approved the change
questions.explanation: The four dimensions are correctness, security, maintainability and human understanding: the person merging must be able to explain what shipped and why. A stronger model or a second AI approval does not show that any human understands the change.
questions.mnemonic: Fourth check is a person: can you explain what shipped?

questions.stem: What does judgment erosion look like in an AI-assisted team?
options: Reviewers rejecting generated code far too often during the review stage
Shipping output nobody fully understands because it looked right and passed checks
Developers refusing to use the tools inside their own editor at all
Escalating nearly every incident to the Architect for resolution
questions.explanation: Judgment erosion is accepting output you no longer understand because it looks plausible and passes checks, until an unreasoned input reaches production.
questions.mnemonic: Looks right, passes checks, nobody understands.

questions.stem: Which stance toward AI-generated code matches the diligence guidance?
options: Apply a lighter bar since the model has already tested its own output
Trust it by default and catch problems later through production monitoring
Relax review somewhat because it ships faster and looks right on inspection
Hold it to the same correctness, security and maintainability standards as hand-written code
questions.explanation: Diligence means the same standards for AI code as any other, especially when it ships faster and looks right. A team without a checklist trusts output by default.
questions.mnemonic: Same bar for AI code as human code.

questions.stem: AI assistance lowers the cost of producing code. What is the consequence for review, and what keeps quality intact?
options: Review volume falls, so fewer checks are needed per change
Review volume rises; a checklist with automated tests and evals holds the bar
Review volume rises, so the Architect must approve every change personally
Review volume stays flat, so only the chosen model tier matters
questions.explanation: Cheaper code production raises the volume reaching review. The checklist defines what must be true, and regression suites and eval sets prove it automatically on every change.
questions.mnemonic: More code in, so automate the gate.

questions.stem: A team has a written verification checklist for AI-generated changes, but reviewers re-derive correctness by hand on every pull request. Which improvement best follows the diligence guidance?
options: Replace the checklist with Claude's own review flags on each pull request
Adopt a vendor-published checklist so the standard is not team-specific
Add a second human reviewer so two people re-check each change by hand
Automate checkable items as a regression suite and eval set gating every change
questions.explanation: Wherever a check can be automatic it should be: a regression suite and eval set turn verification into a gate that runs on every change. The checklist is produced internally for the team's needs, and AI review flags are input, not a verdict.
questions.mnemonic: Checklist says what; tests and evals prove it every time.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe how a verification checklist relates to tests and evals? Select TWO.
options: Once tests and evals exist, the checklist can be retired
The checklist defines what must be true before output reaches production
The checklist should be adopted unchanged from a standard template
Tests and evals prove those properties repeatably on every change
Evals remove the need for the author to understand the change
questions.explanation: The checklist defines what must be true; tests and evals are how the team proves it repeatably instead of by hand. The checklist is team-produced for specific needs, and human understanding remains one of its four dimensions.
questions.mnemonic: Checklist defines, gates prove: both stay.

questions.stem: A team's AI-assisted coding tools are well configured, yet review standards keep slipping on generated changes. What is the hard part of diligence in this situation?
options: Technical: configuring hooks so generated code cannot skip linting
Cultural: holding generated code to the hand-written review standard
Financial: the review budget cannot keep pace with the volume
Technical: choosing a model tier strong enough to skip review
questions.explanation: The hard part is cultural rather than technical: holding AI-generated code to the same review standard as hand-written code, especially when it ships faster and looks right. Better tooling or a stronger model does not remove the need for that standard.
questions.mnemonic: Looks right, ships fast: culture, not tooling, holds the bar.

subjects.title: Operational support, runbooks and escalation
learn: The Architect's support role is translation from symptom to architecture cause, not firefighting.
Gradual quality drop with no code change points to model or prompt change or retrieval drift; compare against an eval set.
Latency spikes: context growth, slow tool or cache not hitting; use traces and token counts. Intermittent tool failures: auth, limits, error paths.
Cost rising without usage change: model tier creep or caching regression; check per-request tier and cache hit rate against the budget model.
Runbooks capture known symptom-to-cause-to-action paths; escalation paths define who handles what and when; the goal is a team needing you only for new problems.
traps: Firefighting instinct: fixing the incident yourself is faster now but repeats the load later.
Slow degradation: a gradual decline no one connects to a cause runs until a scheduled review catches it, not the day it starts.
Cause mismatch: quality drop, latency, tool failures and cost each map to different first actions.
Fix before trace: act on a hypothesis only after tracing evidence, not by changing models first.
Missing boundary: without an escalation path, people do not know what they can resolve.

questions.stem: What is the Architect's core value when an operational issue lands with the team?
options: Replacing the team's on-call rotation with the Architect's own availability
Approving every deploy until incidents stop occurring in production
Connecting the symptom to its architecture cause and teaching the path
Resolving each incident personally and as quickly as possible every time
questions.explanation: The team usually sees a symptom, not a cause. The Architect translates symptom to cause; resolving one incident alone is firefighting rather than lasting support.
questions.mnemonic: Translate the symptom; don't just fight the fire.

questions.stem: Answer quality has declined gradually for weeks with no code change. What is the likely architecture cause and first action?
options: Model or prompt change, or retrieval drift; compare to an eval set
Rate limits; trace one failed call end to end through the tool
A cache stopped hitting; inspect token counts per request
Model tier crept up; check the per-request model tier in use
questions.explanation: Gradual quality decline without code changes points to a model or prompt change or retrieval drift as the corpus grew. Compare to an eval set and check model, prompt and corpus.
questions.mnemonic: Slow slide, no code: eval set, then model, prompt, corpus.

questions.stem: Latency has spiked in a production deployment. What is the best first action?
options: Use traces to find the slowest span: token counts, slowest tool, cache behavior
Switch the whole team to a smaller model immediately to cut latency
Rewrite CLAUDE.md so that the responses become much shorter
Raise the per-user rate cap so requests stop queueing up
questions.explanation: Likely causes are context growth, a slow tool, or a cache that stopped hitting. Traces find the slowest span before any change is made, linking back to production observability.
questions.mnemonic: Find the slowest span before changing anything.

questions.stem: A tool call fails intermittently, and only for some users. Which first action best fits?
options: Re-run the eval set against the current prompt and model version
Check whether retrieval drift set in as the corpus has grown
Compare the per-request model tier against the budget model
Inspect the tool's auth and limits; trace one failed call end to end
questions.explanation: Intermittent tool failures usually trace to authorization, rate limits, or an unhandled error path. Inspect auth and limits and trace a single failed call end to end.
questions.mnemonic: Flaky tool: auth, limits, error path; trace one call.

questions.stem: Spend rose though request volume stayed flat. Which first action is most appropriate?
options: Check per-request model tier and cache hit rate against the budget model
Tighten the escalation path so that cost incidents reach the Architect sooner
Trace the slowest tool call in the request path end to end
Compare the eval set results against those of the previous release
questions.explanation: Cost rising without a usage change suggests model tier crept up or caching regressed. Check per-request tier and cache hit rate against the budget model.
questions.mnemonic: Flat usage, rising cost: tier crept, cache slipped.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a runbook for a deployment?
options: To capture known symptom, cause and action paths for recurring issues
To replace the monitoring dashboards the team already runs
To record who is on call for each weekend and holiday
To document the original architecture decisions for later auditors
questions.explanation: A runbook captures known symptom-to-cause-to-action paths. The symptom-to-cause table is its foundation, letting the team handle recurring issues independently.
questions.mnemonic: Runbook: known symptom, cause, action. No Architect needed.

questions.stem: What does an escalation path define?
options: Which dashboards should be turned red during an incident
Who handles what, and when an issue leaves the team
Which model tier each support ticket is processed on
The weekly report schedule the Architect follows for the team
questions.explanation: An escalation path identifies who handles what and when an issue crosses the team's boundary, so people know what to resolve and what to escalate.
questions.mnemonic: Escalation: who handles what, and when.

questions.stem: Teaching the team a symptom-to-cause path costs more of the Architect's time than fixing one incident directly. Why is it still the right approach?
options: Incidents never recur once the Architect has fixed them once
Teams are prohibited from touching production without the Architect
It is the only support that reduces future load rather than repeating it
It removes the need for the team to keep any runbook
questions.explanation: Teaching costs more up front but is the only version of support that reduces future load. The goal is a team that needs the Architect only for new problems.
questions.mnemonic: Teach once, pay once; fix alone, pay forever.

questions.stem: An Architect could resolve a recurring incident herself in minutes. What is the durable fix?
options: Resolve it personally each time, since speed limits the impact on users
Add more dashboards so the team sees the incident sooner next time
Route every future incident of this kind directly to the Architect
Help the team write a runbook entry and define the escalation path
questions.explanation: The fast fix is to resolve it yourself, but the durable fix is to help the team create a runbook entry and identify the escalation path so it resolves the next occurrence without the Architect. Routing everything to the Architect is firefighting that repeats the load.
questions.mnemonic: Fast fix: do it yourself. Durable fix: runbook plus escalation path.

questions.stem: For a team that owns a production deployment, what is the biggest operational failure mode to guard against?
options: Loud outages that page the whole team at once and force a rushed fix
Excess alerting that gradually wears down the engineers on call
A slow degradation nobody connects to a cause, lasting until a scheduled review
Cost increases hidden because caching quietly masks the real spend
questions.explanation: The biggest failure mode is a slow degradation that no one connects to a cause, so it runs until a scheduled review catches it rather than being caught the day it starts. Loud outages get noticed at once; a runbook entry for gradual decline helps catch the quiet ones.
questions.mnemonic: Quiet slide, no cause linked, waits for the next review.

questions.stem: Which TWO are likely architecture causes of a latency spike? Select TWO.
options: Authorization tokens expired
Context size per request has grown
A cache stopped hitting
Retrieval drift as the corpus grows
The model tier crept up
questions.explanation: Latency spikes trace to context growth, a slow tool, or a cache that stopped hitting. Retrieval drift affects quality, tier creep affects cost, and expired auth causes tool failures.
questions.mnemonic: Slow means big context, slow tool, or cold cache.

questions.stem: Which TWO are likely causes when cost rises without a usage change? Select TWO.
options: An unhandled error path in a tool call
The model tier crept up over time
Retrieval drift as the corpus grew
A new eval set was added to the suite
Caching regressed and hit rate fell
questions.explanation: Cost increases with flat usage point to model tier creep or a caching regression. Error paths cause tool failures and retrieval drift causes quality decline.
questions.mnemonic: Cost up, usage flat: tier crept, cache failed.

questions.stem: A tool used by a production agent fails intermittently. Which THREE are the likely architecture causes? Select THREE.
options: Retrieval drift as the corpus kept growing
An authorization problem on the tool's credentials or scope
Rate limits on the tool being reached under load
The model tier creeping up across requests over time
An unhandled error path in the tool integration
questions.explanation: Intermittent tool failures usually trace to authorization, rate limits or an unhandled error path; the first action is to inspect auth and limits and trace one failed call end to end. Retrieval drift explains gradual quality decline, and tier creep explains cost rising without usage change.
questions.mnemonic: Flaky tool? Auth, limits, unhandled path: trace one failure.
